public_rationale: The August 2024 Andersen ruling preserved Copyright Act claims involving multiple image-generation developers after another contested dismissal round. The December joint filing confirms continuing litigation work. This meets the stated early-resolution rule for the ordinary prediction of sustained copyright disputes. Some claims were dismissed, so the evidence does not support a stronger prediction that developers would lose every case or necessarily owe damages.
limitations: The assessment treats substantial contested proceedings as the ordinary meaning of plenty of legal work.
The cited proceedings establish legal burden, not final infringement liability.
The decisive examples concern U.S. litigation.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: GenAI developers will not easily escape copyright problems, and copyright infringement lawyers will have plenty of work.

statement.excerpt: More than that, GenAI developers won’t get off so easy, and lawyers looking at copyright infringement will still have plenty of work to do.
statement.document_title: No, multimodal ChatGPT is not going to “trivially” solve Generative AI's copyright problems

from_speaker: GenAI developers won’t get off so easy
will still have plenty of work to do
our_interpretation: The plain reading predicts continued substantial copyright disputes requiring sustained legal work across generative-AI developers.
It does not predict that every developer will lose, that every legal theory will succeed, or that damages must exceed a particular amount.
The sentence supplies no deadline. The following sentence's reference to 2024 is assessed separately.
criteria.support_condition: Post-publication records show substantial copyright disputes involving multiple developers continuing through contested proceedings rather than ending promptly.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A decisive industry-wide resolution promptly removes the relevant copyright disputes without substantial further litigation.
